prerequisites: Familiarity with fundamental calculus elements, such as integration and derivation operations
Ability to formulate and solve systems of equations
Basic knowledge of geometry (common curves and surfaces like straight lines, circles, planes, and spheres)

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge of a second language
Basic knowledge of the profession
Ability to solve problems
Oral and written communication in the native language
Skill in the use of ICT
Ability to learn to work autonomously
Understanding and mastery of the basic concepts regarding the general laws of mechanics, thermodynamics, fields and waves, electromagnetism, and their application to solving engineering problems.

Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds upon general secondary education, and is typically at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects implying knowledge from the cutting edge of their field of study.

Students can apply their knowledge to their work or vocation professionally and possess the competencies usually demonstrated through the development and defense of arguments and problem-solving within their field of study.
Students have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific, or ethical issues.
The elaboration and defense of arguments and the resolution of problems within their area of study.
Students have developed the learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

To engage students in teaching activities through the preparation of written assignments, fostering creativity, analytical and synthetic capacity, and information management (bibliographic and internet sources).

To enable students to perform autonomous work and learning, encouraging the use of various bibliographic sources for consultation and analysis in the library. Practical examples will be proposed in theoretical classes for students to solve.
To promote active participation in theoretical classes by solving proposed examples, allowing students to practice the application of specific conceptual competencies.
To train students in experimental data acquisition through laboratory practices, enabling them to apply acquired theoretical knowledge to real problems.
To foster teamwork during practical classes, with at least two students per team to divide experimental measurement tasks.
To encourage autonomous work after laboratory tasks, with each student submitting individual reports, sharing only experimental data.

To comprehend basic Thermodynamics concepts. To understand heat and work as energy transfer forms. To recall the ideal gas concept as an approximation for real gases under specific conditions. To formulate fundamental Thermodynamics principles with practical engineering applications.
To study the concepts and physical description of the electromagnetic field.
To grasp the concept of current.

syllabus_topics: Theme 1. Zero principle. Ideal gas and real gases.
Mayer's Law. Application to ideal gas.
Electrical energy and power. Joule's Law.
Charging and discharging a capacitor through a resistor.
Law of Biot-Savart. Ampère's Law. Applications.
Simple RLC elements under sinusoidal alternating voltage.
teaching_methods: Consultation and analysis of bibliographic sources in the library
assessment_rules: The overall grade is the sum of theoretical (70%) and practical (30%) parts, with a minimum of 5.0 points total to pass. The theoretical part (70%) is assessed via a theoretical exam (50%) and tutorials (20%). The practical part (30%) is assessed via 5 basic written reports (15%), 4 advanced written reports (5%), and a practical written exam (10%). For the single final exam and extraordinary calls, a single written exam covers both theoretical (max 7.0 points) and practical (max 3.0 points) content.
